events.title: Death of Imru al-Qais, 'king of all the Arabs', in Byzantine service

location.name: Palaestina Salutaris (southern Palestine and Nabataean region)

events.summary: A 4th-century tomb inscription, written in Arabic using Nabataean script, names Imru al-Qais as king of all the Arabs and records his death in Byzantine service in 328. Masalha links him to a treaty with Rome as a federate and to rule over Palaestina Salutaris.

sources.author: Nur Masalha

He cites Sartre 2005: 519 for the 328 death date and Fiema et al. 2015: 396-497 for Nabataean Aramaic and Arabic. Masalha also treats him as the Amorkesos of Greek sources (Shahid 1989, 2006a).

perspectives.claim: According to Masalha, the inscription is the first appearance of Ghassanid kings in connection with greater Palestine.

events.editorNote: Date 328 is from the chapter. The chapter does not give the tomb's findspot, so the location is a general region (approximate). The same passage also links Imru al-Qais/Amorkesos with a visit to Emperor Leo I (457-474), which cannot be reconciled with a 328 death; the sequence must be checked against Shahid and Sartre before publication.

events.title: Aspebetos (Petros) becomes first phylarch-bishop of the Palestinian Parembole

location.name: Parembole near the Monastery of Euthymius (between Jerusalem and Jericho)

events.summary: Aspebetos, an Arab chief who had served Persia and then Byzantium, settled near the monastery of Euthymius between Jerusalem and Jericho and was baptised as Petros. About 427 he became the first person to be both Arab phylarch and bishop in Palaestina Prima, according to Masalha.

He cites Shahid 2006a: 181 and Isaac 2003: 450-451 for the phylarch-bishop and Shahid 2006a: 46-48, 181-184, 528 for his later career.

perspectives.claim: According to Masalha, his conversion led to that of his tribe and increased the number of Christian Arabs in Palestine significantly.

events.editorNote: Masalha dates this 'around 427'. Coordinates are a general point on the Jerusalem-Jericho road, approximate; the exact monastery site is not given in the chapter. Cyril of Scythopolis is the underlying source and should be checked.

events.title: Council of Chalcedon separates the Palestines from the Patriarchate of Antioch

location.name: Jerusalem (Patriarchate of Palestine; council held at Chalcedon)

events.summary: At the Council of Chalcedon in 451, the three Palestine provinces were removed from the jurisdiction of the Patriarchate of Antioch. Masalha calls this a turning point; he adds that as Monophysitism spread in the 6th century the Patriarchate remained a stronghold of Greek-led orthodoxy, with lasting effects on Arab-Greek relations in the church.

sources.title: Palestine: A Four Thousand Year History
sources.author: Nur Masalha
sources.note: Printed page numbers estimated from the position in the owner's PDF, calibrated against the book's index (accuracy about 1-2 pages); to be confirmed against the print edition. He cites Shahid 2006a: 528 for the effects on Arab-Greek relations in the Palestine Church.

perspectives.claim: According to Masalha, the separation produced internal conflicts within the Palestine Church that lasted 'until today'.

events.editorNote: The council met at Chalcedon (Asia Minor); the map point is Jerusalem as the seat of the affected patriarchate, so the location is approximate by design. Masalha's reading of long-term consequences is interpretive and needs a second perspective.

events.title: Elias, an Arab-born monk, becomes Patriarch of Jerusalem
events.summary: In 494 Elias, born in Arabia and trained as a monk in the Palestinian desert under Euthymius, became head of the Church in all Palestine as Patriarch of Aelia Capitolina (Jerusalem). Masalha says he improved churches and monasteries and may have helped produce an Arabic liturgy and lectionary.

sources.author: Nur Masalha

sources.title: Elias of Jerusalem
sources.author: Adrian Fortescue
sources.publisher: The Catholic Encyclopedia, vol. 5 (Robert Appleton Company, New York, 1909), via New Advent
sources.note: Arab by birth, educated in an Egyptian monastery, expelled 457, founded a laura near Jericho, ordained priest by Anastasius, succeeded Sallustius as bishop of Jerusalem in 494; resisted Anastasius I's anti-Chalcedonian policy and was banished to Aila (dated 513 here; Wikipedia gives 516).

perspectives.claim: According to Masalha, Elias may also have been associated with translating a simple liturgy and biblical lectionary into Arabic.

events.editorNote: Masalha hedges ('possibly') on the Arabic translation; treat it as unconfirmed. Coordinates for Jerusalem are general knowledge (Holy Sepulchre area).

events.title: Justinian confers phylarchate and titles on Ghassanid leaders

location.name: Palaestina Tertia and Palaestina Secunda (Negev, Petra and Transjordan region)

events.summary: In 529 Emperor Justinian gave Abu Karib ibn Jabalah the phylarchate of Palaestina Tertia, and gave his brother al-Harith ibn Jabalah the highest title open to senators. Al-Harith reigned as Ghassanid king from 528 to 569. Masalha presents these rulers as Arab client kings of parts of Palestine.

sources.author: Nur Masalha
sources.note: Printed page numbers estimated from the position in the owner's PDF, calibrated against the book's index (accuracy about 1-2 pages); to be confirmed against the print edition. He cites Shahid 1989: 69, 89; Shahid 2002: 303; Shahid 1995 vol. 1; Martindale et al. 1992: 111-113; Kazhdan 1991: 163; and Prokopios (hostile to the Ghassanids) via Shahid.

perspectives.claim: According to Masalha, under Ghassanid control the two Palestines functioned effectively as Arab vassal kingdoms.

events.editorNote: Location is a broad region (approximate). The chapter dates al-Harith's kingship to 528 and the title to 529, and the extent of his real control is described as possibly limited at first. Prokopios is a hostile source; Shahid's volumes should be checked directly.

events.title: Muslim forces take Aylah (Aqaba) under Muhammad
events.summary: According to Masalha, Aylah on the Red Sea, the modern port of Aqaba, was the first major town of the Palestine region taken by Muslim forces under the Prophet Muhammad, in 630 (9 AH). He says it later became the province's main trading port to Asia and China.

sources.title: Palestine: A Four Thousand Year History
sources.author: Nur Masalha
sources.note: Printed page numbers estimated from the position in the owner's PDF, calibrated against the book's index (accuracy about 1-2 pages); to be confirmed against the print edition. He cites Ramadan 2010a and 2010b for Aylah's later trade.

perspectives.claim: According to Masalha, Aylah was the first major town in Palestine taken by Muslim forces, under Muhammad in 630.

events.editorNote: Aqaba is now in Jordan; Masalha treats it as part of the province of Jund Filastin. Whether the 630 event was a conquest or a treaty, and its 'first in Palestine' status, should be confirmed with an Islamic-history source. Dated before the 638 era boundary, so classical.

events.title: Battle of Yarmuk: Muslim victory over the Byzantine army
events.summary: After the Battle of Yarmuk in 636, Masalha says Muslim Arab forces overthrew Byzantine rule in the region and ended the Ghassanid phylarchates. He adds that many Monophysite Ghassanids may have preferred the new rulers to the Chalcedonian Church, and that Jabiyah became a main Muslim army camp in Syria.

He cites Shahid 2009 (vol. 2, part 2: 63-64) for the end of the Ghassanid phylarchate and Wigram 2004 for Monophysite attitudes.

perspectives.claim: According to Masalha, the Monophysite Ghassanids 'preferred the Muslim Arab conquerors' to the Chalcedonian Christians.

events.editorNote: Chapter gives only the year and no battle details; the coordinates are an approximate general location on the Yarmuk river (general knowledge). Military details should come from a second source.

events.title: Arab conquest of Aelia Capitolina (Iliya) and the start of Jund Filastin
events.summary: Masalha dates the Arab conquest of Palestine to 638, when Aelia Capitolina became Iliya, later Bayt al-Maqdis and al-Quds. Jund Filastin, the military-administrative province of Palestine, was organised soon afterwards. He argues that Islamisation and Arabisation then proceeded gradually over many generations.

sources.title: Palestine: A Four Thousand Year History
sources.author: Nur Masalha

perspectives.claim: According to Masalha, the Muslim conquest did not reduce the country's prosperity, citing Magness 2003: 13.

Masalha elsewhere says Palestine was brought into the Caliphate in 637-638 (p. 157). The exact date of Jerusalem's surrender is not given. A second source should confirm the date and terms.

events.title: Abd al-Malik's currency reform introduces the Arabic gold dinar
events.summary: Around 696 the Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik introduced the Arabic gold dinar, replacing the Byzantine emperor's image. Masalha says coins struck in Palestine under this system carried the Arabic name Filastin, and that Palestinian cities such as Iliya and al-Ramla later minted coins with 'struck in Filastin'.

perspectives.claim: According to Masalha, local coinage shows a degree of regional Palestinian autonomy under Islam.

events.editorNote: Masalha gives 'around 696'. The exact mint for first Filastin-labelled coins is not stated; the pin is approximate. Masalha's autonomy interpretation is contested and needs a numismatic specialist.

events.title: Al-Aqsa Mosque completed in Jerusalem
events.summary: Masalha dates the completion of the al-Aqsa Mosque to 705, during the Umayyad building programme in Jerusalem. He says it replaced an earlier Islamic mosque on the site and was tied to the Isra and Mi'raj tradition of Muhammad's night journey to Jerusalem, which he places around 621.

He gives the date without a citation in this passage; the Isra and Mi'raj is described as an Islamic tradition.

perspectives.claim: According to Masalha, the mosque was built on an earlier Islamic mosque and is linked to the Isra and Mi'raj.

events.editorNote: Different from the Dome of the Rock event. Completion dates for al-Aqsa vary by source and building phase; verify with archaeological literature. Coordinates are general knowledge.

events.title: Foundation of al-Ramla as the capital of Jund Filastin
events.summary: Suleiman ibn Abd al-Malik, governor of Filastin from 705 to 715, founded al-Ramla as the province's new administrative capital, about 705-715. Masalha says he also built a palace, a mosque and a water system there, and that the city became the country's largest for centuries, with Jerusalem as its religious centre.

perspectives.claim: According to Masalha, the name 'Ramla' more likely commemorates Mu'awiya's daughter Ramla than the Arabic word for sand.

events.title: Fatimids invade and conquer Palestine
events.summary: The Egypt-based Shi'ite Fatimid state invaded Palestine in 970 and had conquered the whole country by 972. Al-Ramla remained the official capital of the province. Masalha describes Fatimid rule as marked by turmoil, tribal revolts, famine and earthquakes, though he notes Islam in Palestine remained largely Sunni.

events.title: Al-Maqdisi completes his geography, Ahsan al-Taqasim
events.summary: In 985 the Jerusalem-born geographer al-Maqdisi finished 'The Best Divisions for Knowledge of the Regions', describing the towns, products and administration of Palestine. Masalha notes that among the names he was known by were 'Jerusalemite' and 'Palestinian', and cites the work for al-Ramla as capital, Jund Filastin's coastal ribats and its economy.

perspectives.claim: According to Masalha, al-Maqdisi's self-description reflects an embryonic regional Palestinian identity.

events.editorNote: Date 985 is from p. 172 (the chapter elsewhere calls it a 10th-century work). The identity reading is interpretive and needs a second source; coordinates are for his native Jerusalem.

events.title: Fatimid caliph al-Hakim orders destruction of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre

location.name: Church of the Holy Sepulchre, Jerusalem

events.summary: In 1009 the Fatimid caliph al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah ordered the destruction of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem and the church of St George at Lydda. Masalha treats this as part of a wider campaign against Christian places of worship in Palestine and Egypt, and as one factor behind later invasions.

sources.author: Nur Masalha
sources.note: Printed page numbers estimated from the position in the owner's PDF, calibrated against the book's index (accuracy about 1-2 pages); to be confirmed against the print edition. He cites Gil 1996 for Fatimid-era conditions.

perspectives.claim: According to Masalha, Fatimid policies spurred local rebellions and the later Seljuk (1073) and Crusader (1099) invasions.

events.editorNote: Masalha's causal link to the First Crusade is interpretive and should be balanced with Crusader-era and Christian sources. Coordinates are general knowledge.

events.title: Banu Tayy tribal revolt and sack of al-Ramla
events.summary: In September 1024 a revolt by the Bedouin Banu Tayy, led by Hassan ibn al-Jarrah, broke out over tax-collection rights in the Beit Jibrin area. The rebels looted Tiberias and occupied and burned al-Ramla. Masalha says the uprisings lingered until 1029 and caused hardship and famine.

sources.note: Printed page numbers estimated from the position in the owner's PDF, calibrated against the book's index (accuracy about 1-2 pages); to be confirmed against the print edition. He cites Lev 2006: 591 and Gil 1996: 22, 25-29; a 1029 letter from Rabbi Solomon ha-Kohen records famine.

events.editorNote: Chapter says the revolt started in September 1024 and Ramla fell later in 1024; month is not exact. The 1025 earthquake is separate. Fatimid/Genizah sources should be checked.

events.title: Fatimid forces defeat Bedouin coalition at al-Uqhuwana
events.summary: In 1029 Anushtakin al-Dizbari, the Fatimid military governor of Palestine, brought an army from Egypt, joined it with local forces, and decisively defeated the combined Bedouin army at al-Uqhuwana near the Sea of Galilee. Masalha says he then united the whole of al-Sham under one Fatimid governor.

sources.author: Nur Masalha
sources.note: Printed page numbers estimated from the position in the owner's PDF, calibrated against the book's index (accuracy about 1-2 pages); to be confirmed against the print edition. He cites Grainger 2016: 246 for the battle and Lev 2003: 55 for al-Dizbari's rule.

events.editorNote: The exact site is not given beyond 'near the Sea of Galilee'; coordinates are approximate (general knowledge). Source for the battle should be checked directly.

events.title: Khair al-Din al-Ramli's fatwa collection is compiled
events.summary: The jurist and landowner Khair al-Din al-Ramli (1585-1671) of Ramla brought his legal opinions together as al-Fatawa al-Khairiyyah. The collection influenced Hanafi jurisprudence across the Arab region and bears on waqf, landholding and agrarian relations. In it he refers to the country as Filastin and to 'our country'.

perspectives.claim: According to Masalha, al-Ramli's use of Filastin for the country shows the territorial notion of Palestine remained alive in local Muslim memory in the early Ottoman period, contradicting claims that the name had been forgotten.

events.editorNote: Masalha says the collection was 'compiled into final form in 1670'; al-Ramli's dates given as 1585-1671. Interpretive claim about the name Filastin rests on Gerber; confirm against Gerber 2008 and a source on the fatwas themselves. Ramla coordinates are general knowledge.

events.title: Al-Tumurtashi of Gaza writes on the Holy Land and Filastin
events.summary: Salih ibn Ahmad al-Tumurtashi of Gaza wrote a work on the Holy Land that also treats the land of Palestine and its boundaries separately from al-Sham. Drawing on the earlier author Mujir al-Din, he placed the borders of Filastin from al-Arish and Rafah in the south to al-Lajjun in the north.

perspectives.claim: According to Masalha, the work shows that al-Sham did not displace the indigenous idea of Filastin; the two terms coexisted and complemented each other.

events.editorNote: Dates 1695-1696 are the dates Masalha attaches to the manuscript (cited as 1695-1696); it is unclear whether this is the composition or the copy date. Masalha says the author died c. 1715. Four copies are said to survive. Gaza coordinates are general knowledge.

events.title: Dahir al-Umar's victory at Marj Ibn Amer
events.summary: After rebelling against Ottoman authority, the Galilee leader Dahir al-Umar al-Zaydani won a military victory at Marj Ibn Amer in 1735. Masalha reports that thousands of local people, including many from Nazareth, then joined his forces, among them Christians who supplied his troops with food and water.

sources.title: Palestine: A Four Thousand Year History
sources.author: Nur Masalha
sources.note: Printed page numbers estimated from the position in the owner's PDF, calibrated against the book's index (accuracy about 1-2 pages); to be confirmed against the print edition. He cites Joudah 1987: 28-31 and Doumani 1995: 42.

perspectives.claim: According to Masalha, the victory followed a successful rebellion against the Ottoman state and helped Dahir become effectively the sovereign ruler of much of Palestine.

events.editorNote: Masalha gives only the year and does not name the opposing force or give the day. A second source (e.g. Joudah 1987, Philipp 2001) should confirm the date, the adversary and the context. Coordinates are an approximate centre of the plain, not a battle site.

events.title: Dahir al-Umar takes Acre and makes it his capital
events.summary: Dahir al-Umar took Acre, then a small port, and made it the seat of his Galilee-based emirate, displacing the older Ottoman province of Sidon. Under him and his successor al-Jazzar the town became fortified and prosperous, a main gateway for cotton and grain exports to Europe.

sources.author: Nur Masalha
sources.note: Printed page numbers estimated from the position in the owner's PDF, calibrated against the book's index (accuracy about 1-2 pages); to be confirmed against the print edition. He cites Philipp 2001: 1, Rosen-Ayalon 1998 and an 1859 British gazetteer.

perspectives.claim: According to Masalha, the pashalik of Acre was a modern creation imposed on the Ottomans by Dahir after he defeated their army, and it later shaped the sanjak of Acre.

events.editorNote: Masalha is inconsistent: pp. 230 and 261 give 1749 for the occupation of Acre, while pp. 223 and 227 say Acre became his capital in 1746. Confirm the date and whether it was military occupation. Coordinates are general knowledge.

events.title: Dahir al-Umar founds 'New Haifa'
events.summary: In 1764-1765 Dahir al-Umar moved the roughly 250 inhabitants of an old hamlet to a walled village about 2.4 km to the east. Called al-Imarah al-Jadidah ('the New Construction'), it became the nucleus of the modern town of Haifa.

sources.title: Palestine: A Four Thousand Year History
sources.author: Nur Masalha
sources.note: Printed page numbers estimated from the position in the owner's PDF, calibrated against the book's index (accuracy about 1-2 pages); to be confirmed against the print edition. He cites Seikaly 2002a, 2002b: 97, Yazbak 1998, Sharon 2013: 262 and Mariti 1792: 318.

perspectives.claim: According to Masalha, the new village grew into an Arab town and later the modern city, and the founding is part of Dahir's building and development programme in northern Palestine.

events.editorNote: Masalha gives 1764-1765 (and 1764-65 in a quotation from Seikaly). Exact site of the old hamlet and of the new village is not given; coordinates are the modern Haifa centre, approximate. Confirm against Yazbak 1998.

events.title: Ottomans recognise Dahir al-Umar's authority in Galilee
events.summary: In 1768 the weakened Ottoman authorities formally acknowledged Dahir al-Umar's position, granting him the title 'Sheikh of Acre, Emir of Nazareth, Tiberias, Safad, and Sheikh of all Galilee'. Masalha compares this to earlier Ottoman recognition of Mount Lebanon's emirate under Fakhr al-Din II.

sources.author: Nur Masalha
sources.note: Printed page numbers estimated from the position in the owner's PDF, calibrated against the book's index (accuracy about 1-2 pages); to be confirmed against the print edition. He cites Philipp 2015 for the title.

perspectives.claim: According to Masalha, the Ottomans were 'forced into a humiliating position' of recognising al-Umar, who remained nominally within the empire while practically sovereign.

events.editorNote: Masalha's wording is interpretive ('forced', 'humiliating'); other historians may describe the grant differently, so a second perspective (e.g. Philipp 2001, Joudah 1987) is needed. Place is Acre as his capital; the act itself would have issued from Istanbul.

events.title: Al-Jazzar Mosque (White Mosque) built in Acre
events.summary: Ahmad Pasha al-Jazzar, who governed the Acre pashalik after Dahir al-Umar, had the White Mosque built in 1781. Its compound included a theological college with student lodging, a court and a library, funded by local taxes and the cotton trade. It remains Acre's best-known landmark.

sources.title: Palestine: A Four Thousand Year History
sources.author: Nur Masalha
sources.note: Printed page numbers estimated from the position in the owner's PDF, calibrated against the book's index (accuracy about 1-2 pages); to be confirmed against the print edition. No direct citation is given for the 1781 date in this passage; Masalha draws on Philipp 2001 and Rosen-Ayalon 1998 nearby.

perspectives.claim: According to Masalha, the mosque is the most monumental symbol of early modern Palestine and of its reorientation towards Europe under al-Umar and al-Jazzar, and its college was the first of its kind in Palestine.

events.editorNote: 'First college of its kind in Palestine' and the al-Azhar model are Masalha's claims; verify against an architectural or historical source. Coordinates are general knowledge for the mosque site in old Acre.

events.title: Jacotin surveys Palestine for Napoleon's maps
events.summary: On Napoleon's orders the French cartographer Pierre Jacotin prepared secret maps of Egypt, Sinai and Palestine in 1799, six of them showing the areas the army crossed. Published in 1826 as the 'Jacotin Atlas', they label the country 'Palestine or Holy Land', with an Arabic label that Masalha renders as 'land of al-Quds'.

sources.author: Nur Masalha
sources.note: Printed page numbers estimated from the position in the owner's PDF, calibrated against the book's index (accuracy about 1-2 pages); to be confirmed against the print edition. He cites Khatib 2003 and Karmon 1960: 155-173, 244-253; he says the Palestine Exploration Fund later published the map (Kallner 1944).

perspectives.claim: According to Masalha, these were the first modern instrumental surveys of Palestine, and the Arabic label echoes in the Ottomans' later creation of the Jerusalem mutasarrifate in 1872.

events.editorNote: Survey year 1799 (campaign February to June); publication 1826. Masalha's Arabic label reads 'land of al-Quds' but the Arabic text is garbled in the extract; verify the exact label. The 'first modern map' claim should be checked. Location is a general centre of the surveyed area.

events.title: Syrian Society renamed the Palestine Association in London
events.summary: A British society founded in March 1805 as the Syrian Society resolved on 24 April 1805 to be called the Palestine Association. Co-founded and led by William Richard Hamilton, it was folded into the Royal Geographical Society in 1834. Masalha sees the renaming as a sign of a growing British separation of Palestine from Syria.

sources.title: Palestine: A Four Thousand Year History
sources.author: Nur Masalha
sources.note: Printed page numbers estimated from the position in the owner's PDF, calibrated against the book's index (accuracy about 1-2 pages); to be confirmed against the print edition. He cites Silberman 1982 and Kark and Goren 2011.

perspectives.claim: According to Masalha, the renaming reflects increasing British evangelical involvement and the beginnings of a British religio-political distinction between Palestine and Syria.

events.editorNote: Event took place in London, outside Palestine; coordinates approximate. The causal link to the French withdrawal and the British naval role in 1799 is Masalha's interpretation. Masalha dates the earlier founding as March 1805. Placed country-wide per the data guide because the event took place or was recorded outside Palestine (original venue: London).

events.title: Palestine Exploration Fund founded in Britain
events.summary: The Palestine Exploration Fund was set up in 1865 by biblical scholars, geographers, military officers and clergy, including Dean Arthur Stanley of Westminster. It sponsored surveys and excavations in Palestine. Its work is credited with advancing knowledge of ancient Jerusalem, though Masalha stresses its links to British strategic interests.

sources.author: Nur Masalha
sources.note: Printed page numbers estimated from the position in the owner's PDF, calibrated against the book's index (accuracy about 1-2 pages); to be confirmed against the print edition. He cites Shepherd 1987 and Goren 2002: 87-110, and quotes the PEF's own website.

sources.title: History
sources.note: Founded 1865 under the royal patronage of Queen Victoria by academics and clergymen, notably Dean Arthur Stanley and George Grove; mission: research into archaeology, history, customs, topography, geology and natural sciences.

perspectives.claim: According to Masalha, its 'scientific exploration' was closely coordinated with the British politico-military establishment and served imperial and strategic aims in the Ottoman East.

events.editorNote: Masalha writes both 1865 and, once, 'the 1860s'. The PEF's own account and historians such as Goren should supply a second perspective on its aims. London coordinates are approximate and the event did not occur in Palestine. Placed country-wide per the data guide because the event took place or was recorded outside Palestine (original venue: London).

events.title: Survey of Western Palestine by the Palestine Exploration Fund
events.summary: Between 1871 and 1877 Royal Engineers working for the Palestine Exploration Fund carried out the Ordnance Survey of Western Palestine, mapping the country and recording place names. Masalha argues that its motives were largely strategic and that its biblical identification of names fed later toponymic projects.

sources.title: Palestine: A Four Thousand Year History
sources.author: Nur Masalha
sources.note: Printed page numbers estimated from the position in the owner's PDF, calibrated against the book's index (accuracy about 1-2 pages); to be confirmed against the print edition. He cites Goren 2002: 87-110, Shepherd 1987, Benvenisti 2002 and Slyomovics 1998.

sources.title: History
sources.note: Lists the Survey of Western Palestine as 1871-1878, conducted by Conder and Kitchener among others.

perspectives.claim: According to Masalha, the survey was mainly driven by Britain's strategic interests rather than the sacredness of Palestine, and its toponymic work underlay later British and Israeli renaming projects.

events.editorNote: Masalha also dates the work 'in the 1870s' and refers to the 1860s earlier Warren explorations (1867-1870). The causal claims about motive and later toponymy are contested interpretation; add a source from PEF or other historians. Location is a general centre of the surveyed area.

events.title: Byzantine Madaba Map is discovered
events.summary: The Byzantine mosaic floor map at Madaba, first partly uncovered in 1884 and recognised in full only in 1896, covers the area from Egypt to Lebanon and carries the name Palaestina in its Greek inscriptions. Masalha notes that Greek Orthodox Patriarchate involvement and publicity from the 1890s to 1906 may have influenced later notions of the country's extent.

sources.title: Palestine: A Four Thousand Year History
sources.author: Nur Masalha
sources.note: Printed page numbers estimated from the position in the owner's PDF, calibrated against the book's index (accuracy about 1-2 pages); to be confirmed against the print edition. He refers to his own chapter four and to a first reproduction made at the Franciscan Printing Press in Jerusalem in 1897.

perspectives.claim: According to Masalha, the discovery and its publicity may have shaped how Yousef al-Issa described Palestine's boundaries in 1912, though he says this is not entirely clear.

events.editorNote: Madaba is in present-day Jordan, outside Palestine proper; included for its role in Palestine representations. Masalha gives 1884 only; the exact day and finders should be confirmed (e.g. Avi-Yonah, Donner). Coordinates are general knowledge.

events.title: Al-Fula land sale to the Jewish National Fund
events.summary: In 1910 Elias Sursuq, a Greek Orthodox banker and absentee landlord in Beirut, agreed to sell the lands of the village of al-Fula in the Nazareth sub-district to the Jewish National Fund. Local peasants petitioned the Ottoman authorities, and Nazareth's district governor Shukri al-Asali backed them in the press, including in Falastin.

sources.title: Palestine: A Four Thousand Year History
sources.author: Nur Masalha
sources.note: Printed page numbers estimated from the position in the owner's PDF, calibrated against the book's index (accuracy about 1-2 pages); to be confirmed against the print edition. He cites Bracy 2011: 45 (quoting Neville Mandel) and Beska 2016b: 4.

perspectives.claim: According to Masalha, the affair became the subject of an intensive newspaper campaign that strongly affected local Arab public opinion and fed opposition to Zionist land purchases.

events.editorNote: Account is from a Palestinian-critical perspective; a Zionist or neutral source (e.g. Mandel, Kark) should confirm the transaction, the outcome for the villagers, and the date of the sale. Village coordinates approximate (modern Afula area); the Sursuq name appears spelt 'Sursuq' in Masalha.

events.title: Israel-Egypt and Israel-Jordan armistice agreements

location.name: Armistice lines (Gaza Strip and West Bank)

events.summary: Under UN auspices, Israel signed armistice agreements with Egypt (24 February 1949) and Jordan (3 April 1949), both at Rhodes. The texts set military demarcation lines, left Egypt in the Gaza area and Jordan in the central highlands, and state that they do not prejudice a final settlement.

sources.title: Egypt-Israel General Armistice Agreement, 24 February 1949
sources.author: Avalon Project, Yale Law School
sources.note: Signing date, place, parties; armistice line described as a military line not to be construed as a political or territorial boundary; Gaza-Rafah line (Arts. V-VI); non-prejudice clauses.

sources.title: Hashemite Jordan Kingdom-Israel General Armistice Agreement, 3 April 1949
sources.author: Avalon Project, Yale Law School

events.title: UN General Assembly Resolution 194 on refugees
events.summary: On 11 December 1948 the UN General Assembly adopted Resolution 194 (III), 35 votes to 15 with 8 abstentions. Paragraph 11 says refugees wishing to return and live at peace should be permitted to, and that others should receive compensation. Its interpretation is disputed.

sources.title: United Nations General Assembly Resolution 194 (text)
sources.author: Wikisource
sources.note: Adoption date and paragraph 11 content (return, compensation, Conciliation Commission tasks).

sources.title: United Nations General Assembly Resolution 194 (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.note: Vote count 35-15-8; Arab, Palestinian and Israeli positions on interpretation; cites Morris, Masalha, Radley, Muravchik, Halevi. Wikipedia used as a secondary pointer only; to be replaced by the underlying works it cites.

perspectives.claim: According to the PLO and Arab states (as summarised by Wikipedia), the resolution is a source of a right of return for refugees.

According to Israeli officials cited there, Israel does not accept an obligation to admit the refugees; Joshua Muravchik argues the text conditions return on being willing to live at peace with neighbours and does not enshrine a right.

events.editorNote: Adopted in Paris; placed country-wide, approximate. Replace Wikipedia with UN document A/RES/194(III) and a scholarly source on interpretation (e.g. Radley 1978, AJIL). The UN digital library PDF was not fetchable.

events.title: Operation Dani: Lydda and Ramle
events.summary: In July 1948, during Operation Dani, Israeli forces took Lydda and Ramle. Tens of thousands of residents left or were driven out. Accounts differ on the death toll in Lydda, on whether the departure was ordered, and on its causes.

sources.title: 1948 Lydda death march (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.note: Chronology 9-13 July 1948; numbers; disputed accounts; cites Morris (1987, 2004), Rabin memoirs, Kadish and Sela, Gelber, Shavit, al-Aref, Pappe, Masalha. Wikipedia used as a secondary pointer only; to be replaced by the underlying works it cites.

perspectives.claim: According to Benny Morris, 50,000-70,000 residents of Lydda and Ramle were expelled, with perhaps 200 killed in the 11 July raid and some 250 in the 12 July fighting around the mosque.
According to Aref al-Aref, 426 people were killed on 12 July, including 176 in the mosque.
According to Alon Kadish and Avraham Sela, there is no direct first-hand evidence of a massacre and the deaths occurred in combat.

events.editorNote: Only a Wikipedia summary read (first 100,000 of 400,000 characters). Needs Morris (1987/2004) and Rabin memoir, plus Kadish and Sela. Coordinates general knowledge; Ramle (31.93, 34.87) is covered by the same event.

events.title: UNRWA established
events.summary: On 8 December 1949 the General Assembly adopted Resolution 302 (IV), creating the UN Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East. It began operations on 1 May 1950, providing direct relief and works programmes to about 750,000 Palestine refugees, according to the UN.

sources.title: United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.note: Resolution 302(IV) of 8 December 1949; abstentions limited to the Soviet bloc and South Africa; about 700,000 refugees served at start; initial relief mandate; Resolution 393(V) reintegration fund. Wikipedia used as a secondary pointer only; to be replaced by the underlying works it cites.

events.title: Absentees' Property Law
events.summary: On 14 March 1950 the Knesset passed the Absentees' Property Law, replacing 1948 emergency regulations. It vested the property of defined 'absentees' in a Custodian. Estimates of the land and buildings affected vary by source.

sources.title: Absentee Property Law (Israel) (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.note: Definition of absentee; Custodian of Absentees' Property; figures; 1973 compensation law; cites COHRE and BADIL, Jiryis, Kedar, Benvenisti, Morris, Israel Government Yearbook 5719. Wikipedia used as a secondary pointer only; to be replaced by the underlying works it cites.

sources.title: Absentees' Property Law, 5710-1950 (text)
sources.publisher: United Nations, UNISPAL (reproducing Laws of the State of Israel, vol. 4, pp. 68-82)
sources.note: Passed 14 March 1950; Sefer Ha-Chukkim No. 37 (20 March 1950) p. 86; s.1(b) absentee; s.2 Custodian; s.4(a) vesting; s.37 replaces 1948 Emergency Regulations from 31 March 1950.

perspectives.claim: According to COHRE and BADIL, an estimated 4.2-5.8 million dunams of land were treated as abandoned.
According to the 1958 Israel Government Yearbook, about 350 abandoned or semi-abandoned villages (roughly 750,000 dunams) and 25,416 buildings were involved.

events.editorNote: Exact day not confirmed in sources read, so year precision. Need the Knesset text and an Israeli-perspective scholarly source.

events.title: Law of Return passed
events.summary: On 5 July 1950 the Knesset unanimously passed the Law of Return, giving Jews the right to immigrate to Israel and obtain citizenship. A 1970 amendment extended eligibility to relatives of Jews. Supporters and critics, including on refugees' return, differ in assessment.

sources.title: Law of Return (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.note: Enactment 5 July 1950, content, 1970 amendment, supporters' and critics' arguments; cites Edelman, Lustick, Yakobson and Rubinstein, ESCWA report. Wikipedia used as a secondary pointer only; to be replaced by the underlying works it cites.

sources.title: Israel's Basic Laws: The Law of Return (text, 1950 and amendments)
sources.note: Passed 5 July 1950, Sefer HaChukkim No. 51 p. 159; s.1 right to come as oleh; Amendment No. 2 (10 March 1970) s.4A extends rights to children, grandchildren and spouses.

perspectives.claim: According to supporters, the law is justified by Jewish persecution and non-Jews can naturalise.
According to Palestinians and refugee advocates, the law contrasts with the denial of a return for Palestinian refugees and is structurally discriminatory.

events.editorNote: Knesset and Jewish Virtual Library pages did not return the text; cite the Knesset text and Lustick (1999) when available. The ESCWA report mentioned was later withdrawn.

events.title: Union of the West Bank with Jordan
events.summary: After the Jericho Conference (December 1948), Jordan formally extended its sovereignty over the West Bank on 24 April 1950. Palestinians there became Jordanian citizens. Britain recognised the union, excluding Jerusalem; the Arab League called it illegal, then treated Jordan as trustee.

sources.title: Jordanian annexation of the West Bank (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.note: Dates, citizenship, recognition by UK and US, Arab League positions; cites Gelber, Benvenisti, Quigley, Aruri, Hansard 27 April 1950. Wikipedia used as a secondary pointer only; to be replaced by the underlying works it cites.

sources.note: Union Act adopted unanimously by the Jordan Assembly 24 April 1950; UK formal recognition, but not of Jordanian sovereignty in the Jerusalem area (de facto authority only).

events.editorNote: Wikipedia only; 'union' vs 'annexation' is itself contested. Replace with Hansard 1950 and Gelber (2004). Coordinates approximate.

events.title: Gaza Strip under Egyptian administration
events.summary: From the 1948 war until June 1967, Egypt administered the Gaza Strip. The All-Palestine Government, declared in September 1948, had a largely symbolic role. Egypt did not annex Gaza or grant citizenship; UNRWA provided aid to the large refugee population.

sources.title: All-Palestine Government (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.note: Egyptian administration, status, refugees, 1959 annulment; cites Shlaim 1990, Gelber, Kassim, Shehadeh, UN Doc S/1264/Corr.1. Wikipedia used as a secondary pointer only; to be replaced by the underlying works it cites.

sources.note: Defines the Gaza-Rafah armistice line within which Egyptian forces remained.

events.editorNote: Start month is the 22 Sept 1948 declaration; Egyptian military presence predates it. End month June 1967. Replace Wikipedia with Shlaim (1990) JPS article.

events.title: Kafr Qasem killings
events.summary: On the eve of the Sinai campaign, Israeli Border Police shot villagers returning to Kafr Qasem, an Arab village inside Israel, during a curfew. Forty-eight villagers were killed, or 49 in counts that include an unborn child. In 1958 a military court convicted eight men of killing 43 of them; sentences were later cut.

sources.title: Kafr Qasim massacre (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.note: Date, 48-49 deaths, curfew, court-martial of 11, eight convictions on 16 Oct 1958, Shadmi fined 10 prutot, all out by Nov 1959; cites Robinson, Bilsky, Sorek, Haaretz. Wikipedia used as a secondary pointer only; to be replaced by the underlying works it cites.

sources.title: Military Tribunal Terms Shooting Order in Kfar Kassem "illegal"
sources.note: Eight border policemen found guilty of killing 43 Arabs; order termed illegal.

sources.author: Danny Orbach
sources.publisher: International Journal of Middle East Studies 45(3), 2013, pp. 491-511 (Cambridge University Press)
sources.note: Abstract read: the trial established the doctrine of a 'manifestly unlawful order'. Full text paywalled.

perspectives.claim: According to the Israeli court-martial, as summarised, the order to shoot curfew violators was manifestly illegal.

events.editorNote: Title avoids the loaded term 'massacre' used by the source article; an Israeli or academic source (Bilsky 2004; Robinson 2013) is needed. Britannica and B'Tselem fetches failed (403/429). Coordinates general knowledge.

events.title: Killings in Khan Yunis and Rafah
events.summary: During Israel's occupation of the Gaza Strip in the 1956 Suez war, many Palestinians were killed in Khan Yunis (3 November) and Rafah camp (12 November). UNRWA's December 1956 report listed 275 names for Khan Yunis and 111 for Rafah; Palestinian sources give 415 for Khan Yunis. Israeli authorities said there was resistance.

sources.title: Khan Yunis massacre (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.note: Dates; UNRWA Dec 1956 report of 275 names; Morris estimate; Palestinian sources 415 killed and 57 missing; Israeli account; cites UNRWA A/3212/Add.1, Morris 1994, Filiu, Sacco. Wikipedia used as a secondary pointer only; to be replaced by the underlying works it cites.

sources.title: Special Report of the Director of UNRWA covering the period 1 November 1956 to mid-December 1956 (A/3212/Add.1)
sources.note: Khan Yunis occupied 3 Nov: lists of 275 named dead (140 refugees, 135 residents); Rafah camp 12 Nov screening operation: 111 named dead; Israeli claim of resistance vs refugees' denial.

perspectives.claim: According to UNRWA's December 1956 report, lists of names numbered 275 people allegedly killed on 3 November.
According to Israeli accounts cited, soldiers met armed militants and a battle followed.

events.editorNote: Wikipedia only; the UNRWA report A/3212/Add.1 and Morris, Israel's Border Wars (1994) must be read. Rafah date (12 Nov) is Morris's; Rafah has a separate toll. Title avoids 'massacre'.

events.title: Suez Crisis and Israeli Sinai campaign
events.summary: On 29 October 1956 Israeli forces attacked across Sinai. Britain and France then landed troops, citing protection of the Suez Canal. Under US pressure they accepted a UN ceasefire on 6 November. The Gaza Strip was occupied by Israel during the fighting.

sources.title: Suez Crisis, 1956
sources.author: Office of the Historian, US Department of State
sources.note: Chronology 26 July-6 November 1956; Israeli attack 29 October; Anglo-French landing; UN ceasefire; US role.

sources.title: Khan Yunis massacre (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.note: Israel took Khan Yunis on 3 November 1956 (Gaza occupation). Wikipedia used as a secondary pointer only; to be replaced by the underlying works it cites.

sources.title: Special Report of the Director of UNRWA covering the period 1 November 1956 to mid-December 1956 (A/3212/Add.1)
sources.note: Israeli forces attacked the Gaza Strip on 1 November 1956; UNRWA operations under the occupying Israeli authorities.

events.editorNote: The State Department page does not mention Gaza or UNEF; Israel's Gaza occupation and the 1957 withdrawal need a source (e.g. UN GA resolutions of 1956-57, Morris 1994). Placed approximate on Gaza.

events.title: Palestine Liberation Organization founded
events.summary: Following an Arab League initiative, the first Palestinian National Council met in Jerusalem on 28 May 1964 and established the PLO under Ahmad Shuqayri. Its 1964 charter set Arab unity and the liberation of Palestine as complementary goals.

sources.title: Palestine Liberation Organization (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.note: Arab League initiative; council in Jerusalem 28 May 1964; some sources date founding 2 June; Shukeiri; cites Masri. Wikipedia used as a secondary pointer only; to be replaced by the underlying works it cites.

sources.title: Statement of Proclamation of the Organization (Jerusalem, 28 May 1964)
sources.author: Ahmad Shukairy, First Arab Palestinian Congress
sources.publisher: Permanent Observer Mission of Palestine to the UN (archived)
sources.note: Proclamation dated 28 May 1964 in Jerusalem; the congress closed on 2 June 1964.

events.editorNote: Wikipedia only (first 100,000 characters). 28 May vs 2 June needs confirmation from Sayigh (1997) or the Palestinian National Charter. Britannica fetch failed. Coordinates general knowledge.

events.title: Israeli raid on as-Samu
events.summary: On 13 November 1966 Israeli forces raided as-Samu in the southern West Bank, then under Jordan, after a mine killed three Israeli soldiers on 12 November. On 25 November the UN Security Council censured Israel in Resolution 228.

sources.title: Security Council Resolution 228 (1966)
sources.author: United Nations Security Council
sources.note: Date 25 November 1966, vote 14-0-1 (New Zealand abstaining); censure of Israel for violating the UN Charter and the 1949 armistice agreement.

sources.title: Samu Incident (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.note: Raid details, casualty and house-destruction estimates (40-125 houses); US, Jordanian and Israeli views. Wikipedia used as a secondary pointer only; to be replaced by the underlying works it cites.

perspectives.claim: According to Prime Minister Eshkol, the raid answered sabotage originating from Jordan.

perspectives.viewpoint: US National Security Adviser Walt Rostow
perspectives.claim: According to Rostow, the raid was out of all proportion to the provocation.

events.editorNote: Casualty figures from Wikipedia only; replace with UN report. Resolution text was summarised by the fetch tool, not read verbatim. Coordinates general knowledge.

events.title: June 1967 war: Israel occupies the West Bank, Gaza Strip, Sinai and Golan
events.summary: Fighting between Israel and Egypt, Jordan and Syria from 5 to 10 June 1967 ended with Israel in control of the West Bank including East Jerusalem, the Gaza Strip, the Sinai Peninsula and the Golan Heights. The causes and the question of who bore responsibility are debated.

sources.title: Arab-Israeli War of 1967 (Milestones)
sources.author: Office of the Historian, U.S. Department of State
sources.note: Supports: sequence from 13 May (Soviet warning, Egyptian troop moves), 16 May UNEF withdrawal request, 22 May closure of the Straits of Tiran, war 5-10 June, territories occupied, and that some U.S. advisers judged U.S. interests were best served if Israel acted alone.

perspectives.claim: According to the Office of the Historian, Palestinian raids and Israeli reprisals, the Soviet false report of Israeli troop concentrations, Egypt's expulsion of UNEF and the closure of the Straits of Tiran preceded the war, and some of President Johnson's advisers concluded that U.S. interests would be best served if Israel acted alone.

events.editorNote: Only one source read (Britannica returned 403). The central dispute (pre-emptive self-defence versus avoidable war) needs named scholars from both sides, e.g. Michael Oren, Avi Shlaim, Tom Segev, Ahron Bregman, plus a Palestinian or Arab source; not yet read. Coordinates are a general-knowledge centre of the occupied areas.

events.title: UN Security Council adopts Resolution 242

location.name: Palestine (decided at UN Security Council, New York)

events.summary: On 22 November 1967 the Security Council adopted Resolution 242, calling for withdrawal of Israeli forces from territories occupied in the recent conflict and a just settlement of the refugee problem. The wording of the withdrawal clause has been interpreted differently by the parties.

sources.title: United Nations Security Council Resolution 242 (1967)
sources.author: United Nations Security Council
sources.note: Supports: adoption date 22 November 1967 and the wording of the withdrawal and refugee clauses.

sources.title: Arab-Israeli War of 1967 (Milestones)
sources.author: Office of the Historian, U.S. Department of State
sources.note: Supports: that Israelis and Arabs interpreted the resolution differently, and its role as basis for 'land for peace' diplomacy.

perspectives.claim: According to the Office of the Historian, Israelis and Arabs interpreted the resolution differently, and U.S. officials believed Israel should not withdraw until peace settlements were in place.

events.editorNote: Decided in New York; placed country-wide. The interpretive dispute (English versus French text) is not yet sourced; add specific Israeli and Arab/Palestinian statements. Coordinates general knowledge.

events.title: 'Imwas, Yalu and Beit Nuba depopulated and demolished
events.summary: In June 1967 the residents of the villages of 'Imwas, Yalu and Beit Nuba, near Latrun, were ordered out and the villages were later demolished. Israel later established Canada Park on the land. Accounts differ on how the departure occurred and on its justification.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Imwas
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.note: Last-resort source, flagged for replacement. Supports: 7 June 1967 depopulation, population figures (1961 Jordanian census 1,955), demolition and Canada Park. The article cites Rich Wiles, Behind the Wall (2010); Tom Segev, 1967 (2007); Michael Oren, Six Days of War (2002); Mayhew and Adams, Publish It Not (2006). Those works should be read for page cites.

perspectives.claim: According to Wiles, residents were ordered by megaphone to leave and march toward Ramallah, and the houses were then destroyed.
According to Segev, Israeli newspapers at the time depicted the flight as voluntary, and Central Command orders described the demolitions as punishing 'the nest of murderers'.
According to Oren, as summarised on Wikipedia, Israel justified the expulsion by citing alleged residents' roles in 1948 attacks on Jerusalem and an Egyptian commando raid on Lod.

events.editorNote: Wikipedia only, and its own page carries a cleanup tag. Total displaced is given by Wiles as about 8,000 for the three villages, unverified. Yalu and Beit Nuba need own population data. Coordinates are general knowledge for Imwas. Needs a B'Tselem, Segev or Israeli-army-archive source.

events.title: Allon Plan and the first Israeli settlements in the occupied territories
events.summary: After June 1967 Israeli minister Yigal Allon proposed that Israel keep the Jordan Valley, East Jerusalem and the Etzion Bloc. The cabinet never formally adopted the plan, but settlement in the first decade largely followed it.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Allon Plan
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.note: Last-resort source, flagged for replacement. Supports: plan content, never officially endorsed, settlements along the Jordan Valley, Kiryat Arba approved 1969. The article cites B'Tselem (2011), Human Rights Watch (2010), FRUS 1964-1968, Haaretz 2007 and Kimmerling and Migdal, The Palestinian People (2009).

perspectives.viewpoint: Wikipedia summary of the plan's history
perspectives.claim: According to the article, King Hussein rejected the plan, and settlement policy in the first decade of occupation was largely based on it even though successive Israeli cabinets never officially endorsed it.

events.editorNote: Year of plan (mid-1967 draft, revised 1968) and the dates of Kfar Etzion (1967) and Kiryat Arba (1968-70) need a primary source; not asserted. Legal status of settlements (ICJ 2004, UN SC 465) should be added with the Israeli government position.

events.title: Battle of Karameh
events.summary: On 21 March 1968 Israeli forces attacked the Karameh camp in Jordan, held by Fatah and the Jordanian army. Casualty figures vary by source. Both sides claimed success, and Fatah's prestige and recruitment grew afterward.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Battle of Karameh
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.note: Last-resort source, flagged for replacement. Supports: date, forces, casualty range by author, and competing interpretations. Cited there: Herzog and Gazit; Pollack, Arabs at War (2002); Morris, Righteous Victims (1999); Teveth, The Cursed Blessing; Maoz, Defending the Holy Land (2006).

sources.title: United Nations Security Council Resolution 248 (1968)
sources.note: Adopted unanimously 24 March 1968; condemns Israel's large-scale military action on Jordanian territory.

perspectives.claim: According to Morris (as summarised on Wikipedia), Israel lost 33 dead and 161 wounded, and the PLO 156 dead and 141 captured.
According to Chaim Herzog, 28 Israelis were killed and 69 wounded, and 200 PLO fighters killed.
According to the article, Palestinian and Arab accounts treat it as a psychological victory, and Fatah reported about 5,000 applicants within 48 hours.

events.editorNote: Wikipedia only; replace with Morris, Shlaim or Britannica (403). Coordinates general knowledge for Karameh (Jordan Valley, east bank); outside Palestine proper but part of the PLO story. Security Council Resolution 248 (1968) should be read.

events.title: Black September: Jordanian army and the Palestinian fedayeen
events.summary: In September 1970 King Hussein ordered the Jordanian army against Palestinian guerrilla groups after aircraft hijackings. Fighting lasted until 27 September; casualty estimates range widely. Guerrilla presence in Jordan ended in 1971 and the PLO relocated to Lebanon.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Black September
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.note: Last-resort source, flagged for replacement. Supports: dates (main fighting 16-27 Sept 1970, wider conflict until July 1971), causes, and casualty range. Cited there: Avi Shlaim, Lion of Jordan (2008); Massad, Colonial Effects (2001); Kissinger, Years of Renewal.

perspectives.claim: According to Massad, about 3,400 PLO members were killed; the article gives the range as 2,000 to 3,400 and says Arafat's claim of 25,000 is not corroborated.
According to the Jordanian Armed Forces, 537 Jordanian soldiers were killed.

events.editorNote: Wikipedia only; page read only to the first 100,000 characters. Place is Jordan (outside Palestine), coordinates general knowledge for Amman. Needs Shlaim and a Palestinian source in print with pages.

events.title: Land Day protests in the Galilee
events.summary: On 30 March 1976 Arab citizens of Israel held a general strike and demonstrations against a plan to expropriate land in the Galilee. Six Arab demonstrators were killed and about a hundred wounded. 30 March is commemorated annually as Land Day.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Land Day
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.note: Last-resort source, flagged for replacement. Supports: the expropriation plan of about 20,000 dunams between Sakhnin and Arraba (6,300 dunams Arab-owned), six deaths, about 100 wounded, and commemoration. Cited there include Abdo and Lentin (2002), Kimmerling and Migdal, McDowall (1990), Yiftachel (2006), Haaretz, BBC.

perspectives.claim: According to Abdo and Lentin, three of the dead were women.
According to a 2003 Israeli government document cited in the article, protesters burned tires, blocked roads and threw rocks and Molotov cocktails.

events.editorNote: Wikipedia only. Sakhnin used as focal location (deaths occurred in several towns; confirm). Need an Israeli primary source for the 1976 expropriation order.

events.title: UN General Assembly Resolution 3236 on the rights of the Palestinian people

events.summary: On 22 November 1974 the General Assembly reaffirmed the Palestinian people's right to self-determination, national independence and return, by 89 votes to 8 with 37 abstentions, and asked for contacts with the Palestine Liberation Organization.

events.title: Camp David Accords and the Egypt-Israel peace treaty

location.name: Sinai and Palestine (negotiated at Camp David, USA)

events.summary: Egypt and Israel signed the Camp David frameworks on 17 September 1978 and a peace treaty on 26 March 1979, ending the state of war and returning Sinai to Egypt. The frameworks proposed five-year transitional Palestinian self-government; the follow-on talks stalled.

sources.title: Treaty of Peace between Egypt and Israel (1979)
sources.author: Egypt and Israel

sources.title: Camp David Accords (Milestones)
sources.author: Office of the Historian, U.S. Department of State
sources.note: Supports: that Israel rejected full withdrawal from the West Bank and Gaza, that parties disagreed on the application of Resolution 242 and on settlements, and that autonomy talks stalled after Palestinian representatives declined to take part.

perspectives.claim: According to the Office of the Historian, the delegations disagreed over whether Resolution 242 applied to the territories and over the status of settlements, and the autonomy negotiations stalled when Palestinian representatives refused to take part.

events.editorNote: Palestinian and PLO rejection of the framework is not sourced from a Palestinian-perspective source yet; add. Placed country-wide; coordinates general knowledge.

events.title: Israel invades Lebanon and besieges Beirut
events.summary: On 6 June 1982 Israel launched 'Operation Peace for Galilee' into Lebanon after the shooting of its ambassador in London. Israeli forces besieged Beirut, and the PLO leadership and fighters were evacuated in August under international supervision.

sources.title: Wikipedia: 1982 Lebanon War
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.note: Last-resort source, flagged for replacement. Supports: start date 6 June 1982, Argov shooting on 3 June, stated aims, siege and PLO evacuation. Cited there: Maoz; Morris; Shlaim; Fisk; Pollack. End date 29 September 1982 is the article's date for the Israeli operation; troops stayed until 1985.

perspectives.claim: According to Maoz (as summarised on Wikipedia), Defence Minister Ariel Sharon's goals included destroying PLO infrastructure in Lebanon, expelling Syrian forces and installing a Christian-led government.
According to the article, the publicly stated aim was to push PLO forces about 40 km from the border.

events.editorNote: Wikipedia only; casualty totals deliberately left out as sources differ widely (infobox gives 654 Israeli dead; PLO 1,000-2,400). August evacuation dates not read. Needs Shlaim or Morris with pages.

events.title: Killings in the Sabra and Shatila camps, Beirut
events.summary: From 16 to 18 September 1982 Lebanese Forces militiamen killed civilians in Sabra and Shatila while Israeli forces surrounded the area. Estimates of the dead range from about 460 to over 3,000. Israel's Kahan Commission found Israel indirectly responsible.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Sabra and Shatila massacre
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.note: Last-resort source, flagged for replacement. Supports: dates, perpetrators, Israeli role, casualty estimates by author, Kahan Commission findings, UN GA Resolution 37/123 (vote 123-0-22 on section D). The article uses the word 'massacre' in its title; this entry avoids it in our own voice.

perspectives.claim: According to the Palestinian Red Crescent, more than 2,000 people were killed.
According to al-Hout, at least 1,300 victims were named, with a possible total of up to 3,500.
According to Israeli intelligence estimates, 700 to 800 were killed.
According to Germanos, 460 were killed.

According to the Kahan Commission (February 1983), Israeli military personnel failed to take serious steps to stop the killings and the IDF bore indirect responsibility; it found Defence Minister Sharon personally responsible for ignoring the danger of bloodshed.
According to Resolution 37/123 (16 December 1982), the Assembly condemned the killings and described them as an act of genocide.

events.editorNote: Wikipedia only; read the Kahan report itself (Avalon link returned 404) and the UN text to replace. Range in summary runs from Germanos (460) to Kapeliouk (about 3,000-3,500). Coordinates general knowledge.

events.title: First intifada begins
events.summary: A Palestinian uprising against the Israeli occupation began in the Gaza Strip on 9 December 1987 after a road accident killed four Palestinians. It spread to the West Bank with strikes, boycotts and stone-throwing. The end date is disputed between 1991 and 1993.

sources.title: Wikipedia: First Intifada
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.note: Last-resort source, flagged for replacement. Supports: trigger, forms of protest, casualty counts and end date options. Cited there include B'Tselem statistics, Benny Morris Righteous Victims (2001), Shlaim, Human Rights Watch, Wendy Pearlman (2011), Mary King A Quiet Revolution (2007). Page read to the first 100,000 characters.

perspectives.claim: According to B'Tselem, Israeli security forces killed 1,087 Palestinians (other counts: 1,204 and 1,284), and Palestinians killed 100 Israeli civilians and 60 soldiers.

perspectives.viewpoint: Associated Press and Israel Defense Forces
perspectives.claim: According to the Associated Press an estimated 771, and according to the IDF 942, Palestinians were killed by other Palestinians as suspected collaborators.
According to the article, Palestinians believed the road accident was retaliation for an Israeli's killing in Gaza; Israel denied this.

events.editorNote: Trigger incident is dated 8 December and the start 9 December by sources. Wikipedia only; B'Tselem statistics page returned 429 and should be fetched. End date 13 Sept 1993 is the infobox date (Oslo signing); some sources end it at Madrid 1991. Coordinates general knowledge.

events.title: Palestine National Council proclaims the State of Palestine
events.summary: On 15 November 1988 the Palestine National Council, meeting in Algiers, proclaimed the State of Palestine with Jerusalem as capital, citing the 1947 partition resolution; the vote was 253 to 46 with 10 abstentions. The UN General Assembly later acknowledged it by resolution 43/177.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Palestinian Declaration of Independence
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.note: Last-resort source, flagged for replacement. Supports: date and place, PNC vote 253-46-10, text drafted by Mahmoud Darwish, UNGA 43/177 vote (104 for, 2 against, 44 abstentions) and recognition counts. Primary text not yet read.

sources.title: UN General Assembly Resolution 43/177 (text)
sources.note: Acknowledges the proclamation of the State of Palestine by the PNC on 15 November 1988; 'Palestine' designation from 15 December 1988.

events.editorNote: Wikipedia only; primary text (Avalon URL returned 404) to be read. Placed country-wide; venue Algiers in summary. Claim that the 1988 PNC statement accepted Resolution 242 needs a primary source; Israeli and US reactions not yet sourced.

events.title: Madrid Conference opens Arab-Israeli negotiations
events.summary: From 30 October to 1 November 1991 Spain hosted a conference co-sponsored by the United States and the Soviet Union. Palestinians took part in a joint delegation with Jordan, without declared PLO members. It launched bilateral and multilateral negotiation tracks.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Madrid Conference of 1991
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.note: Last-resort source, flagged for replacement. Supports: dates, participants, delegation conditions (Haidar Abdel-Shafi led it; Israel objected to PLO members, East Jerusalem residents and outsiders), the two tracks and Washington talks from December 1991. Cites Oren (2007), Lasensky (2002), Harms and Ferry (2005), Journal of Palestine Studies (1992).

perspectives.claim: According to Harms and Ferry, the conference's symbolic significance far outweighed its concrete accomplishments.

events.editorNote: Wikipedia only (history.state.gov page returned 404). Add primary invitation letter and a Palestinian account. Placed country-wide; coordinates general knowledge.

events.title: Israel and the PLO sign the Oslo Declaration of Principles
events.summary: Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organization signed the Declaration of Principles on interim self-government in Washington, D.C. It provided for a Palestinian interim authority and a five-year transition, and deferred Jerusalem, refugees, settlements and borders to later talks. Mutual recognition was exchanged beforehand.

events.title: Attack on worshippers at the Ibrahimi Mosque, Hebron

location.name: Hebron (Ibrahimi Mosque / Cave of the Patriarchs)

events.summary: Baruch Goldstein, a settler from Kiryat Arba, opened fire on Muslim worshippers at the Ibrahimi Mosque/Cave of the Patriarchs, killing at least 29 before being killed. An Israeli commission led by Meir Shamgar found he acted alone; the site was later divided between Muslim and Jewish worship.

sources.title: Hebron massacre inquiry exonerates government, IDF; blames Goldstein only
sources.author: Jewish Telegraphic Agency
sources.note: Supports: at least 29 killed, Shamgar Commission findings (Goldstein acted alone, lax security, unclear open-fire orders), recommendations, and the criticisms from the Israeli left, settlers and Palestinian leaders.

sources.title: Scars of massacre still fresh in Hebron
sources.author: Al Jazeera
sources.note: Supports: 29 worshippers killed, roughly twice that number injured, nearly two-month curfew, division of the mosque interior and the 1996 H1/H2 division; Palestinian perspective on the aftermath.

perspectives.claim: According to the Shamgar Commission, the killings were the act of one man, and no negligence by government officials or senior officers was found.
According to Hebron's mayor, Mustafa Natshe, speaking after the report, the army did nothing and the settlers remained.
According to Al Jazeera, the Palestinian population of the old town fell from an estimated 30,000 to a few thousand after curfews and closures, many of them forced out.

events.editorNote: Number wounded not firmly sourced (Al Jazeera says about twice the dead); confirm with the Shamgar report or B'Tselem. Terminology: title avoids 'massacre'; sources use it. Coordinates are general knowledge for the Ibrahimi Mosque.

events.title: Israel-Jordan peace treaty signed at the Arava crossing
events.summary: Prime Ministers Yitzhak Rabin and Abdul Salam Majali signed a peace treaty fixing the Israel-Jordan boundary, allocating water, and recognising Jordan's special role over Muslim shrines in Jerusalem. The boundary with the West Bank was set 'without prejudice' to that territory's status.

sources.title: Israel-Jordan peace treaty
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.note: Wikipedia used as a last resort and flagged as such. Supports: signing date and place, signatories, Jerusalem shrines clause, boundary description, water allocation (50 million cubic metres per year to Jordan).

events.title: Oslo II Interim Agreement divides the West Bank into Areas A, B and C
events.summary: Rabin and Arafat signed the Interim Agreement in Washington, extending Palestinian self-rule in the West Bank. It created Areas A, B and C with different mixes of Palestinian and Israeli authority, and Area C was to be transferred in phases. Area C remains under Israeli control; OCHA put it at about 62% of the West Bank in 2010.

sources.title: Oslo II Accord
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.note: Wikipedia used as a last resort and flagged as such. Supports: initialled at Taba on 24 September, signed 28 September 1995 by Rabin and Arafat, five-year interim period, permanent-status talks to begin by 4 May 1996. Page gives no area percentages.

sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.note: Wikipedia used as a last resort and flagged as such. Supports: Area C about 60% of the West Bank under exclusive Israeli control; settler population rising from about 115,700 to 203,000 between 1993 and 2000 (as stated there).

sources.title: Area C of the West Bank: Key Humanitarian Concerns (update August 2014)
sources.note: Read. Over 60 percent of the West Bank is Area C, where Israel retains near exclusive control; about 300,000 Palestinians and some 341,000 settlers in Area C.

events.title: Camp David summit of July 2000
events.summary: President Clinton hosted Ehud Barak and Yasser Arafat at Camp David, Maryland, to seek a final settlement. No agreement was reached, with Jerusalem and the Haram al-Sharif, refugees and territory the main disputes. Participants and scholars give conflicting accounts of who was responsible for the failure.

sources.title: 2000 Camp David Summit: Background and Overview
sources.author: Jewish Virtual Library
sources.note: Supports: dates 11-24 July 2000, participants, and the account (relying heavily on Dennis Ross) that Arafat rejected proposals without a counter-offer. Pro-Israel site; Ross, Ben-Ami, Clinton and Barak cited.

sources.title: Summary of Malley and Agha's argument (as reported in the Jewish Virtual Library overview)
sources.author: Robert Malley and Hussein Agha (summarised)
sources.note: I could not open Malley and Agha's own text (NY Review of Books URL returned 404); only this secondary summary. Replace with the primary article.

sources.title: Camp David: The Tragedy of Errors
sources.publisher: Robert Malley and Hussein Agha, The New York Review of Books, 9 August 2001
sources.note: Read in full. Arafat feared a trap; Israeli and US tactical errors; also faults the Palestinians for giving no counterproposal; Haram al-Sharif custodianship ideas.

perspectives.claim: According to Dennis Ross, Arafat rejected the proposals and offered no counter-proposal, and the responsibility lay with Arafat rather than Barak and Clinton, though Ross acknowledged tactical mistakes by the U.S. and Israel.

According to Malley and Agha, Israeli and US tactical errors and Arafat's belief that he faced a trap contributed to the failure, though they also fault the Palestinians for offering no counterproposal.

events.editorNote: Contested; the only sources read are both via one pro-Israel site. Needs primary participant accounts from the Palestinian side (e.g. Malley/Agha, Abu Ala or Erekat) and Israeli (Ben-Ami). Venue is in Maryland; placed country-wide (approximate).

events.title: Sharon's Haram al-Sharif visit and the start of the Second Intifada
events.summary: Ariel Sharon, then Likud opposition leader, visited the Haram al-Sharif/Temple Mount under heavy police guard. Clashes followed the next day and grew into an uprising lasting until about 2005. The Mitchell Committee (2001) found the visit 'poorly timed' but not its cause. B'Tselem counted 3,174 Palestinians and 940 Israelis killed to the end of 2004.

sources.title: Second Intifada
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.note: Wikipedia used as a last resort and flagged as such. Supports: date of the visit, Likud spokesman's stated purpose, Israeli and Palestinian readings of causes, Marwan Barghouti's statement, casualty ranges 29 Sept 2000 - 1 Jan 2005 (Israelis about 1,010; Palestinians 3,179-3,354), end date 8 February 2005 (Sharm el-Sheikh). Only the first third of the page was read.

sources.title: Sharm el-Sheikh Fact-Finding Committee Report (Mitchell Report)
sources.publisher: Avalon Project, Yale Law School (report dated 30 April 2001)
sources.note: Read. Visit on 28 Sep; lethal police force on 29 Sep; GOI and PLO accounts of causes; the visit did not cause the intifada but was poorly timed; no persuasive evidence of a PA plan or that the visit was more than an internal political act.

sources.title: 2004: Hundreds die at Israel's hand
sources.publisher: Al Jazeera, 3 January 2005 (reporting B'Tselem's annual figures)
sources.note: Read. Per B'Tselem: 3,174 Palestinians (617 minors) killed by Israeli forces and settlers and 940 Israelis killed, September 2000 to end 2004. Article wording is not neutral; use only for the attributed figures.

perspectives.claim: According to many Palestinian and Arab commentators cited, Sharon knew the visit could provoke violence and it was a political act.
According to Israeli authorities cited, a waqf official's loudspeaker call led to the stone-throwing that followed.
According to Marwan Barghouti, the uprising would have erupted even without the visit.

events.editorNote: Casualty figures vary widely by source; replace with B'Tselem and Israeli MFA/Shin Bet tallies read directly (B'Tselem page returned 429). Wikipedia flagged. Coordinates general knowledge for the plateau.

events.title: West Bank barrier approved; ICJ advisory opinion of 9 July 2004
events.summary: Israel began building a barrier in June 2002, saying it prevents attacks from the West Bank. About 85% of the route runs inside the West Bank (OCHA, 2016). On 9 July 2004 the International Court of Justice found, by 14 votes to 1, the sections in occupied territory, including East Jerusalem, contrary to international law; Israel disputed the Court's jurisdiction.

sources.title: West Bank Barrier
sources.author: UN OCHA oPt
sources.note: Supports: government approval in 2002, planned length 712 km, about 465 km (65.3%) completed as of 2016, about 85% of route inside the West Bank, Israel's stated rationale, ICJ 9 July 2004 finding, reported humanitarian impacts.

sources.title: Legal Consequences of the Construction of a Wall in the Occupied Palestinian Territory (Advisory Opinion, 9 July 2004)
sources.author: International Court of Justice
sources.note: Supports: Court's conclusions (wall and regime contrary to international law, obstructs self-determination, Israel must cease construction and make reparation, States must not recognise); rejected self-defence and necessity. Page does not show the vote or Israel's arguments.

sources.title: Israeli West Bank barrier
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.note: Wikipedia used as a last resort and flagged as such. Supports: 23 June 2002 approval; Israeli claim of fewer suicide bombings (73 in 2000 to July 2003 vs 12 Aug 2003 to end 2006); Israeli Supreme Court rulings 30 June 2004 and 15 September 2005; Palestinian objections.

sources.title: Legal Consequences of the Construction of a Wall in the Occupied Palestinian Territory: Advisory Opinion (ICJ Press Release 2004/28)
sources.publisher: UNISPAL copy of ICJ Press Release 2004/28, 9 July 2004

perspectives.claim: According to Israel, the barrier is intended to prevent attacks by Palestinians inside Israel.
According to the ICJ, the wall and its associated regime in the occupied territory are contrary to international law.
According to Palestinian leaders cited, the barrier seizes land, separates communities and amounts to de facto annexation.

events.title: Israeli disengagement from Gaza
events.summary: Israel removed about 8,475 settlers from 21 Gaza settlements and four in the northern West Bank, and withdrew its ground forces, completing this on 12 September 2005. Israel holds that this ended its occupation of Gaza; the UN and others hold that Israel's control of airspace, waters and crossings kept it in place.

sources.title: Israeli disengagement from Gaza
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.note: Wikipedia used as a last resort and flagged as such. Supports: dates, about 8,475 settlers, 21 Gaza settlements plus Kadim, Ganim, Homesh, Sa-Nur, disputed occupation status, and Dov Weissglass's October 2004 statement. Only first third of the page read.

sources.title: Israel's Disengagement from Gaza (CRS Report RS22000)

perspectives.claim: According to Israel, the withdrawal of its ground presence ended its occupation of Gaza.

perspectives.viewpoint: UN and human rights organisations (as summarised)

According to a quotation attributed to Weissglass in October 2004, the plan's significance was 'the freezing of the peace process'.

events.title: UN General Assembly grants Palestine non-member observer state status
events.summary: On 29 November 2012 the General Assembly adopted resolution 67/19 in New York by 138 votes to 9, with 41 abstentions. It accorded Palestine non-member observer State status, without prejudice to the role of the PLO as representative of the Palestinian people. Israel, the United States and seven other States voted against.

sources.title: United Nations General Assembly Resolution 67/19
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.note: Wikipedia used as a last resort and flagged as such. Supports: date, vote (138-9-41, 5 absent), the nine States voting against, Netanyahu's and Nuland's statements, Israel's housing announcement afterward.

events.editorNote: Only Wikipedia read (UN press and digital-library pages returned 403/errors); confirm the vote and text on the UN Digital Library (A/RES/67/19). Voted in New York; placed country-wide (approximate).

events.title: ICJ advisory opinion on Israel's policies and practices in the occupied territory
events.summary: On 19 July 2024 the International Court of Justice gave the General Assembly an advisory opinion. By 11 votes to 4 it found Israel's continued presence in the occupied Palestinian territory unlawful, to be ended as rapidly as possible; by 14 to 1, that Israel must stop new settlement, evacuate settlers and make reparation. The opinion is not binding.

sources.title: Legal Consequences arising from the Policies and Practices of Israel in the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including East Jerusalem (Advisory Opinion, 19 July 2024)
sources.author: International Court of Justice

sources.author: IHL Centre (formerly Diakonia)

sources.title: ICJ's Advisory Opinion - Legal Consequences arising from the Policies and Practices of Israel in the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including East Jerusalem
sources.note: Read. Operative paragraph with votes: jurisdiction unanimous; 14-1 to comply; 11-4 unlawful presence and obligation to end it (against Sebutinde, Tomka, Abraham, Aurescu); 14-1 settlements and reparation; 12-3 non-recognition by States and international organisations.

events.title: Lake Hula and its marshes are drained
events.summary: From 1951 to 1958 the Jewish National Fund drained Lake Hula, which had covered 12-14 square kilometres, and the marshes around it. The stated aims were to reduce malaria-carrying mosquitoes and to create farmland. The peat later burned and blew away, endemic fish were lost, and in the early 1990s part of the valley was flooded again.
events.details: An Ottoman concession to drain the marsh dates from 1908 and the Palestine Land Development Company bought it in 1933. The lake was about 5.3 km long and 4.4 km wide, 1.5 to 3 m deep. A small papyrus reserve was set aside in 1963 and the Hula Nature Reserve opened in 1964.

events.summary: The Dead Sea covered about 1,050 square kilometres in 1930 and about 605 in 2016; in 2025 its surface stood 439.78 metres below sea level. Wikipedia reports it has shrunk by about a third since the 1960s, partly because less Jordan water arrives, and that sinkholes have opened along its shores.
